planting.note: Broadcast seed on shallow, rocky calcareous soil in fall so winter freeze-thaw cycles work it into the surface; avoid covering seed deeply.

directions: Black sagebrush is a compact, slow-growing dwarf shrub of the thinnest, rockiest soils in Great Basin sagebrush steppe, distinguished from big sagebrush by its shorter stature, darker evergreen foliage, and preference for shallow lithic sites where few other shrubs can root. Tiny three-toothed leaves release a sharp, resinous aroma when brushed, and inconspicuous yellow flower spikes appear in late summer. It is used extensively in high-desert restoration and low-water landscaping where its tight, uniform habit reads almost like a dwarf conifer. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; it resents any supplemental irrigation or fertile ground once past its first year.

planting.note: Fall-broadcast seed on moist drainage bottoms or swale edges within sagebrush steppe; tolerates heavier, less-drained soil than big sagebrush.

directions: Silver sagebrush occupies the moister swales, stream terraces, and seasonally wet flats within the sagebrush steppe mosaic, forming dense colonies from spreading rhizomes rather than the solitary stature typical of big sagebrush. Its narrow, silvery, undivided leaves and suckering habit make it useful for stabilizing streambanks and disturbed drainage edges in restoration plantings. It tolerates periodic saturation and somewhat heavier soils better than its upland relatives, while still demanding excellent drought tolerance through the dry summer months. Mow or cut back old growth occasionally to keep colonies from becoming woody and open at the base.

planting.note: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly in fall for strong spring establishment; sod-forming rhizomes fill in bare ground faster than bunchgrass neighbors.

directions: Thickspike wheatgrass is a rhizomatous sod-forming grass scattered through Great Basin sagebrush steppe, spreading by underground stems into a tight turf that resists both drought and foot traffic once mature. Narrow blue-green blades stay low and dense through the growing season, with slender seed spikes rising only modestly above the foliage in early summer. Its sod-binding habit makes it one of the most effective native grasses for stabilizing disturbed slopes, roadcuts, and erosion-prone rangeland, and it recovers well after grazing or mowing. It needs no irrigation once established and performs poorly in constantly wet or heavily shaded ground.

planting.note: Fall-sow on lean alkaline or sandy soil to allow winter chilling to break seed dormancy; avoid rich or amended ground.

directions: Spiny hopsage is a rounded, spine-tipped shrub of alkaline flats and sagebrush steppe margins across the Great Basin, valued by wildlife managers as nutritious winter and spring browse for pronghorn and mule deer. Small gray-green leaves emerge early in spring alongside inconspicuous flowers, and female plants develop showy clusters of papery, rose-to-salmon winged fruits by early summer that give the shrub real ornamental interest in restoration and wildlife gardens. It thrives in the leanest, most alkaline or saline soils where few other woody plants persist, and requires no supplemental water once established. Avoid heavy or frequently irrigated soils, which quickly lead to root failure.

planting.note: Fall-sow or cold-stratify before spring planting on lean, gravelly soil in full sun; seed needs winter chilling to germinate reliably.

directions: Silverleaf phacelia forms low mounds of felted, silvery-gray lance-shaped leaves scattered through sagebrush steppe and dry rocky slopes of the Intermountain West, with coiled clusters of small lavender-to-white flowers unfurling along the stem tips through late spring and early summer. The dense, soft pubescence that gives the foliage its silvery cast also helps the plant shed excess sun and conserve moisture through the dry season. It is a strong early-season nectar source for native bees in high-desert pollinator gardens and seed mixes, performing best in lean, fast-draining gravelly or sandy soil. Avoid fertile or regularly irrigated garden beds, which shorten its lifespan and encourage floppy growth.

planting.note: Fall-sow and leave exposed to winter cold on gravelly, lime-rich soil; germination is slow and erratic without a full cold stratification period.

directions: Carpet phlox forms tight, spine-tipped cushions barely a couple of inches tall that hug the ground across the stoniest, most exposed flats of Great Basin sagebrush steppe, often blooming while snow patches still linger nearby. Masses of small white-to-lavender flowers nearly cover the foliage for a brief but showy burst in earliest spring, making it a favorite of rock gardeners seeking authentic high-desert cushion plants. It demands razor-sharp drainage and resents any organic mulch or summer water, which quickly rot the tightly packed stems. Use it in scree beds, trough gardens, or gravel pavements where its dense mat can be viewed up close.
